# Cam and camshaft (`cam_camshaft`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: helped by water_wheel
- Core idea: A cam is a projection or shaped disc on a rotating shaft that pushes a lever or rod aside once per turn and then lets it go or guides it back. Pegs on a water wheel shaft lift a hammer, a stamp or a bellows board and drop it; several cams set at different angles round one shaft work several hammers in turn and spread the load evenly. A smoothly shaped cam gives any timed motion wanted: the tunes of a musical automaton, the valves of an engine. It is the simplest way to turn rotation into repeated strokes, needing no crank.
- Pitfalls:
  - All cams in line, so every hammer lifts at once and the wheel stalls
  - A sharp-edged cam and follower that dig into each other; round and grease them
  - Expecting a cam to push a heavy load both ways; it lifts, and weight or a spring returns
- History: greece: 3rd c. BC–1st c. AD – cams in Alexandrian automata (Philo, Hero); china: c. 20 AD – cam-lifted water-powered trip hammers (Huan Tan); rome: 1st–2nd c. AD – cam-driven ore stamps inferred from worn anvil stones at Spanish and Welsh gold mines; islamic: 1206 – al-Jazari's camshafts in automata and water-raising machines; europe: 11th–12th c. – cams in fulling and hammer mills; 15th c. stamp mills and pegged-barrel musical automata
- Read:
  - Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 4 Part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965)
  - al-Jazari, The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices (1206; tr. Donald R. Hill, 1974)
